title: Abram in the idol shop
hookLine: midrash asks what the text leaves unsaid, and answers with a story
carry: midrash answers the torah's silences with stories
tomorrow: what did God look at before making the world?

cards: Fan fiction, deleted scenes, the prequel nobody asked for and everybody watched: people can't leave a gap in a story alone. The rabbis couldn't either.
The new block is midrash, and midrash begins exactly in the gaps, in what a text leaves unsaid. Today, one well-known gap, and the story that fills it.

teach.h: GET THEE OUT. BUT WHY HIM?
teach.b: Here's a well-known gap. Genesis twelve opens with God telling Abram: "Get thee out of thy country." No introduction.
No reason why him. The Torah doesn't say. So a midrash, in Genesis Rabbah, tells a story about Abram's family.
One day Abram minds the shop. A woman brings a plate of fine flour as an offering. Abram takes a stick, smashes every idol but the biggest, and puts the stick in its hand.
His father comes back: what happened here? Abram says the big one got hungry and broke the rest. Terah snaps: they can't do anything!
And Abram answers: listen to what your own mouth is saying. That's midrash: a question the text raises, answered with a story. The word comes from a root meaning to seek.
The story sits beside the verse, not inside it.

teach.h: MIDRASH ANSWERS THE TORAH'S SILENCES WITH STORIES.
teach.b: Now one last look down the road just finished, since this is a review day too: truth because it's true; sick with love; slowly toward love; love grows with knowing; a plan to return; always possible.
Six lines from a law book that kept asking what love would do.

how: Midrash is read in Jewish study and retold to children; the story of Abraham and the idols, from Genesis Rabbah, is a classic in Hebrew schools and family retellings.

games.q: your little cousin asks: 'did Abraham really smash the idols? it's not in my Bible.' what's the honest answer?
o: it's a midrash: a rabbis' story filling a gap the Torah leaves.
yes, it's in Genesis, just a few chapters later.
nobody tells that story; someone must have made it up.
games.why: the story comes from Genesis Rabbah. the Torah leaves the gap; the midrash answers it with a story and sets it beside the verse.

practice: Choose a story you know well: a family story, a scene from a favorite book. Ask it, out loud, one question it never answers: why did she leave? what did he say on the walk home?
Don't answer it yet; let the question sit in the room with you.
